title: Academic Inbreeding and Collaboration Patterns: A Comparative Publication Profile of Two Turkish Universities
text_snippet: Academic Inbreeding and Collaboration Patterns: A Comparative Publication Profile of Two Turkish Universities ABSTRACT This study examines how academic inbreeding relates to scientific collaboration through a publication‐level comparison of two Turkish universities during 2018–2022: Hacettepe University, a long‐established, research‐intensive public university and TED University, a young foundation university. Using AVESİS publication records ( N = 6292) and staff profiles ( N = 1371), authors are classified into two mobility profiles, distinguishing those with international degree or work experience from those whose education and employment are entirely domestic. A publication‐level inbreeding category is then assigned according to whether author teams comprise only one profile or combine both. Collaboration is measured across six co‐authorship settings, and internationally co‐authored publications are further classified by the World Bank income group of partner countries. Findings reveal a marked institutional contrast. At Hacettepe, domestic collaborations are predominantly produced by teams composed entirely of authors with domestic‐only education and work experience. title: From Compliance to Co‐Production: Developing a Sector‐Informed Equality Impact Analysis Framework for Inclusive Governance in Higher Education
text_snippet: From Compliance to Co‐Production: Developing a Sector‐Informed Equality Impact Analysis Framework for Inclusive Governance in Higher Education ABSTRACT Equality Impact Assessments (EqIAs) in higher education are often perceived as bureaucratic exercises rather than tools for transformative change. This paper presents research on the existing use of EqIAs across Britain, including key challenges, and an exploration of the value of the coproduction of EqIAs. It utilises the findings to inform the contribution of an evidence‐based, holistic and context‐driven framework. Research underpinning this paper explores how participatory approaches can reposition EqIAs from compliance‐driven processes towards inclusive governance. This paper draws on multi‐phase qualitative research with marginalised voices and Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) leads across England, Scotland and Wales. Findings reveal widespread inconsistency in EqIA application, limited integration into institutional strategy and perceptions of disproportionate burden. Core barriers to effective use include insufficient resources, poor understanding among decision‐makers and tokenistic consultation with marginalised communities. title: Institutional Logics and the Strategies and Practices of Interdisciplinary Research Centres: Competition or Convergence?
text_snippet: Institutional Logics and the Strategies and Practices of Interdisciplinary Research Centres: Competition or Convergence? ABSTRACT Drawing on data from two interdisciplinary research centres in a German university, this study seeks to understand the extent to which different institutional logics influence the strategies and practices of interdisciplinary research centres, as well as how university actors accommodate the various logics in their work. Professional logics were predominant in shaping the work practices of academics, whereas market and industry logics played a larger role for middle management, especially in establishing the credibility of interdisciplinary research in terms of its capacity to generate external funding. Reflecting a managerial logic, interdisciplinarity was framed as a way to enhance the profile and international reputation of the university. The convergence of professional and market and industry logics was most salient during the process of seeking funding, as well as during centre meetings when directors and academics sought to establish how scientific interests were aligned with the priorities of external funders and industry partners.

title: Systematic Review of the Global Patterns and Determinants of International Student Mobility
text_snippet: Systematic Review of the Global Patterns and Determinants of International Student Mobility ABSTRACT This systematic literature review synthesizes and analyses a corpus of 140 studies on the size and flows of international student mobility (ISM), as well as its determinants. The review confirms a consistent global increase in international students, albeit experienced differently in terms of magnitude by certain regions and countries. However, it also shows how ISM is decentralizing and diversifying, diluting the traditional East–West flows against the acceleration of regional mobility and the emergence of hubs. While criticizing the incomplete theorisation of ISM research, the review combines the push‐pull factor approach with an examination of individual factors to analyse determinants. Findings show that individual factors and push factors have been under‐researched compared to pull factors. Individual factors foreground students' agency, as these are not simply reactive to external conditions when making decisions. Despite limitations, such as sampling methods or data availability and comparability, the review captures state‐of‐the‐art knowledge on ISM and suggests future research avenues. title: Academic Peer Network Effects of Doctoral Students: An Empirical Research Based on Response‐Driven Sampling in China
text_snippet: Academic Peer Network Effects of Doctoral Students: An Empirical Research Based on Response‐Driven Sampling in China ABSTRACT This study used Response‐Driven Sampling (RDS) to construct an academic peer network for PhD students in China and conducted a questionnaire survey. After testing 639 valid samples that met the random recruitment assumption, empirical analysis was conducted on academic peer network effects on the research competence of PhD candidates (RCPC). The results show that RCPC is significantly influenced by academic peer network size, homogeneity, and peer competence. (1) Peer competence demonstrates the strongest positive effect on RCPC, particularly for those with low initial research competence. (2) In comparison, the effect of network homogeneity is relatively smaller and predominantly negative. The homogeneity between PhD students and their academic peers remains relatively low across the sample, with all values below 0.7. (3) The network size of weak ties does not significantly affect RCPC. However, among strong ties, the number of peers from other departments and universities exhibits an inverted U‐shaped relationship with self‐assessed competence, with the optimal network size being 16 peers. title: Understanding Early Academic Careers Through the Lens of Psychological Precarity: A Qualitative Longitudinal Study
text_snippet: Understanding Early Academic Careers Through the Lens of Psychological Precarity: A Qualitative Longitudinal Study ABSTRACT For many early‐career academics (ECAs), unstable and short‐term contracts are a major contributor to employment precarity. However, even when job security improves, feelings of professional and personal insecurity often persist. This study uses psychological precarity as an analytical lens to examine how such insecurity is experienced and internalised, shaped not only by employment conditions but also by institutional culture, role ambiguity, and the search for professional legitimacy. A reflexive thematic analysis of longitudinal focus group data with 12 early career researchers over a 12‐month period in a higher education institution was conducted. Five themes were identified: (1) the persistence of psychological precarity beyond job security; (2) systemic drivers of precarity; (3) navigating the boundaries of an ill‐defined role and workload; (4) relational supports and complexities; and (5) the search for work‐related value and meaning. Rather than identifying new forms of insecurity, the findings demonstrate how employment insecurity, organisational ambiguity, identity, and relational dynamics interact to produce enduring experiences of psychological precarity. title: Global Citizenship Education for Peace in Politically Sensitive Contexts: Research Integrity, Knowledge Diplomacy and Censorship
text_snippet: Global Citizenship Education for Peace in Politically Sensitive Contexts: Research Integrity, Knowledge Diplomacy and Censorship ABSTRACT This paper responds to two politically charged reactions to my scholarship on peace and global citizenship education (GCE): the censorship of a UNESCO Beijing conference presentation in Seoul (August 2025) and a confrontational exchange with a Chinese postgraduate student in New Zealand. Drawing on literature on research integrity, politicisation and the conceptual framework of knowledge diplomacy, I examine how scholarship on conflict‐affected societies is reframed through nationalist narratives that equate “neutrality” with silence and erasure. The censored study presents a qualitative comparative analysis of 40 faculty in China/Taiwan, Cyprus, Korea and Somalia/Somaliland, informed by the “local turn” in peacebuilding and postcritical theory. It finds that understandings of peace and GCE are contextually grounded: educators in recognised states foreground sameness, while those in contested contexts foster dialogue across difference. In this paper, I examine the study's contested reception and defend dialogic academic freedom as essential to research integrity and knowledge diplomacy.

title: The Gender Pay Gap in Asia: Examining Awareness and Policy Endorsement Among Postgraduate Students in the Higher Education Sector
text_snippet: The Gender Pay Gap in Asia: Examining Awareness and Policy Endorsement Among Postgraduate Students in the Higher Education Sector ABSTRACT The persistent gender pay gap (GPG) remains a critical issue in higher education institutions (HEIs), yet little is known about the mechanisms that drive student support for systemic policy change. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), this study examines how Asian postgraduate students awareness of the GPG shapes their views on benefits, barriers, causes and institutional policy solutions. Data for this study were collected from 212 postgraduate students across various disciplines. The findings confirm that higher GPG awareness is positively associated with stronger support for policy interventions. This awareness is also linked to greater recognition of the GPG's structural and institutional causes and a stronger belief in the benefits of its closure. Crucially, students who attribute the GPG to structural causes demonstrate stronger support for government policy interventions. Furthermore, the perceived causes of the GPG significantly mediate the relationship between awareness and policy support.

title: Reconfiguring University Missions in the Knowledge Society: The Case of Portuguese Universities in European Alliances
text_snippet: Reconfiguring University Missions in the Knowledge Society: The Case of Portuguese Universities in European Alliances ABSTRACT This paper examines how European Knowledge Society policy scripts, amplified by the European Universities initiative, are appropriated in the strategic plans of Portuguese public universities. Focusing on nine universities participating in European Universities Alliances, it asks how they position the ‘relationship with society’ in mission narratives, whether they prioritise commercial or civic/socially responsive engagement, and what patterns of convergence, local translation and decoupling emerge. The study combines a two‐stage document analysis: frequency‐based semantic analysis of mission‐related terms and qualitative content analysis of strategic plans. Findings show that societal engagement is now central to mission discourse, often alongside teaching and research. However, institutions differ markedly: some emphasise commercialisation, innovation and knowledge transfer; others stress civic responsibility, social cohesion, culture and sustainability; most combine both. The paper argues that these hybrid narratives reflect adaptive responses to multiple legitimacy pressures rather than inconsistency or failure.

title: Motivation to Pursue a Master's Degree, Approaches to Learning and Perceived Employability
text_snippet: Motivation to Pursue a Master's Degree, Approaches to Learning and Perceived Employability ABSTRACT Perceived employability is a key learning outcome for higher education students who wish to advance their careers after graduation. Most studies of perceived employability have focused on undergraduate students; little attention has been paid to master's students. Given the increasing number of master's students and their diverse employment needs, this study examined the relationships among motivation, approaches to learning, and perceived employability. Following a cross‐sectional design, data were collected from 786 master's students across various programmes and institutions in Hong Kong and analysed using structural equation modelling. By measuring perceived employability as the outcome variable, the results revealed that master's students with higher intrinsic motivation were more likely to adopt a deep approach to learning, while those with higher extrinsic motivation were more likely to adopt a surface approach. The results indicated that approaches to learning fully mediated the association between intrinsic motivation and perceived employability. title: Governing Internal Innovation in Higher Education: Evidence From a 5‐Year President‐Led Challenge Program
text_snippet: Governing Internal Innovation in Higher Education: Evidence From a 5‐Year President‐Led Challenge Program ABSTRACT Universities are under increasing pressure to convert strategic priorities into participatory and sustained internal change. This study examines a 5‐year president‐led challenge program at a private Latin American university as a governance mechanism for internal innovation. Drawing on annual program documentation, a consolidated participant database covering 3772 applicant records and 2738 unique individuals, implementation‐tracking records, and documented lessons learned, the analysis examines how challenge themes, participant profiles, winner profiles, and implementation trajectories evolved from 2021 to 2025. Findings show a shift from pandemic continuity and student transition issues toward inclusion, sustainability, mobility, wellbeing and artificial intelligence governance. Applicant and winner profiles differed significantly in every year, suggesting recognition was associated with changing forms of expertise and institutional proximity rather than simple participation volume. title: Evaluating the Sustainable Competitiveness of Asian Education Hubs: A Dual‐Diamond Index System
text_snippet: Evaluating the Sustainable Competitiveness of Asian Education Hubs: A Dual‐Diamond Index System ABSTRACT The rapid proliferation of education hubs throughout Asia underscores the need for a robust analytical framework to evaluate their long‐term sustainability and competitiveness. This study addresses this gap by proposing a novel Dual‐Diamond model, which integrates Porter's Theory of Competitive Advantage with a Context‐Input‐Process‐Output (CIPO) framework to assess the Sustainable Competitiveness of Education Hubs (SCEH). Employing a mixed‐methods approach that combines expert consultation and the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), a quantifiable Education Hub Sustainable Competitiveness Index (EHSCI) was developed, comprising 28 indicators across four dimensions. Application of Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) to data from 12 Asian education hub countries reveals a distinct core‐periphery spatial pattern. Furthermore, the analysis identifies two systemic configurations—termed ‘regular’ and ‘irregular’ diamond systems—which reflect contrasting strategies for sustaining competitiveness, characterized respectively by balanced synergistic development or concentrated strategic strengths. title: Zone‐Based Transnational Education: Beyond Knowledge Diplomacy and Soft Power Frameworks
text_snippet: Zone‐Based Transnational Education: Beyond Knowledge Diplomacy and Soft Power Frameworks ABSTRACT Transnational education (TNE) is typically theorized through Jane Knight's knowledge diplomacy framework, which emphasizes cooperation and mutual benefit, or Jenny Lee's soft power perspective, which highlights geopolitical competition. This article argues that both frameworks fail to explain zone‐based TNE, where universities operate within Special Economic Zones explicitly designed for capital accumulation. Drawing on Quinn Slobodian's analysis of zones, this article examines Deakin University's campus in Gujarat International Finance Tec‐City (GIFT City), India as an illustrative case of how zone‐based TNE operates through transnational capitalist coordination rather than diplomatic or strategic purposes. The GIFT City case reveals three reconfigurations: capital interests predominate over diplomatic ideals; universities minimize regulatory oversight through an asymmetric arrangement; and educational provision becomes human capital development for zone‐based employment. Unlike non‐zone TNE, these reconfigurations are structurally embedded in the zone's design rather than negotiated case by case, constituting a qualitatively distinct form of internationalization. title: Grasping Sustainability Culture in Higher Education Institutions: Conceptualizing and Understanding Key Elements
text_snippet: Grasping Sustainability Culture in Higher Education Institutions: Conceptualizing and Understanding Key Elements ABSTRACT This study addresses the limitations of structural reforms in higher education institutions (HEIs) by emphasizing the need for a robust sustainability culture to support long‐term transformation. Despite growing interest, the concept of sustainability culture is still underdefined, leading to fragmented practices and a lack of shared orientation. To clarify this concept, the study applies a culture‐theoretical framework and combines literature review with expert interviews to examine what constitutes sustainability culture in HEIs and how to identify it. The analysis indicates that participatory structures, respectful work environments, and transparent communication are critical cultural conditions that shape the effectiveness of sustainability efforts. By defining and translating these dimensions into observable indicators, the study contributes to organizational theory in the context of sustainability and provides practical guidance for institutional development. It demonstrates that cultural initiatives are essential complements to structural strategies and that a mature sustainability culture fosters well‐being and collaboration within and across institutions.

title: How Professional Curricula Shape Undergraduate Employability in the Generative AI Era: Evidence From Career Planning Documents
text_snippet: How Professional Curricula Shape Undergraduate Employability in the Generative AI Era: Evidence From Career Planning Documents ABSTRACT The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is significantly transforming the professional landscape, necessitating a reevaluation of how professional curricula foster undergraduate employability. While most existing studies rely on structured scales to explore linear causal relationships, this approach limits the ability to capture students' career readiness when navigating the technological disruptions introduced by GenAI. To fill this research gap, our study examines 36 undergraduate career planning documents as authentic evidence of students' career readiness. Utilising a data‐driven text mining approach, we uncover the underlying patterns of students' career strategies in the GenAI era. The research findings indicate the following: (1) Students' career readiness can be categorised into four typical adaptation profiles: goal‐oriented, experience‐driven, skill‐based and context‐anticipatory. title: Taboos in Doctoral Socialisation: Learnings From the Indian Context
text_snippet: Taboos in Doctoral Socialisation: Learnings From the Indian Context ABSTRACT This paper explores taboos in doctoral socialisation in India. The qualitative study draws on 20 text‐based survey responses, 11 online interviews with current and recent PhD graduates and 20 social media snippets collected through netnography. Using the framework of Student Socialisation in Higher Education, the paper reveals three interlinked pathways through which taboos distort the doctoral socialisation process: (1) dysfunctional interactions with primary socialisation agents (supervisors and peers), (2) perverse integration into a culture of silence and submission and (3) the internalisation of hardship as a virtue—what we have called ‘learning to see the PhD journey as Tapasya’. We propose the concept of ‘malignant socialisation’ to describe a process in which students who have negative doctoral experiences are not failing to socialise but are being socialised successfully into a dysfunctional culture. Four properties define this malignancy: self‐perpetuation, the framing of harm as virtue: a cultural residue, structural rationality of silence and cultural legitimation. title: Understanding Entrepreneurial Intentions in Higher Education: Students' Perceptions and Experiences in Hong Kong
text_snippet: Understanding Entrepreneurial Intentions in Higher Education: Students' Perceptions and Experiences in Hong Kong ABSTRACT Universities worldwide are expanding entrepreneurship education, yet less is known about how students understand entrepreneurship and what factors shape their entrepreneurial intentions. Drawing on survey data from 561 undergraduate students across diverse disciplines and institutions in Hong Kong, this study examines students' perceptions of entrepreneurship, their participation in entrepreneurship‐related learning, and variations in entrepreneurial intention. The findings show that entrepreneurship is rarely seen as an immediate post‐graduation career choice, although longer‐term intention varies considerably across students. Respondents commonly viewed entrepreneurship both as new venture creation and as a means of achieving social impact and personal development. Participation was concentrated in knowledge‐oriented learning activities, while action‐oriented experiences were relatively rare, suggesting a gap between interest and practical readiness. Non‐STEM students reported higher entrepreneurial intention than STEM students, whereas differences by gender, family income and academic performance were not statistically significant. title: Advancing Outward‐Oriented Internationalisation of Higher Education Through Development Assistance: Malaysia's Evolution and Future Outlooks
text_snippet: Advancing Outward‐Oriented Internationalisation of Higher Education Through Development Assistance: Malaysia's Evolution and Future Outlooks ABSTRACT As an emerging donor in the Global South, Malaysia has increasingly advanced development assistance (DA) through its internationalisation of higher education (IHE) agenda. DA can be understood as a policy domain at the intersection of HE and foreign policy, requiring alignment between the two agendas. Assessing how these policies and practices have evolved in the Malaysian HE sector is therefore important for generating evidence‐based insights into future strategic directions, particularly as Malaysia advances towards developed‐nation status. Adopting a historical approach, this article traces the development of Malaysia's DA‐HE policies and practices through the lens of outward‐oriented internationalisation of higher education (OIHE). Malaysia's DA‐HE trajectory across four phases: the first phase marks the establishment of technical cooperation as the core instrument of DA–HE engagement; the second reflects its embedding within IHE policy; the third captures diversification through innovative and multilateral modalities; and the fourth signals a stronger strategic alignment with global prominence and educational diplomacy. title: A Shared Turn, Divergent Logics: A Comparison of International Student Employment Policies in China, Japan and Korea
text_snippet: A Shared Turn, Divergent Logics: A Comparison of International Student Employment Policies in China, Japan and Korea ABSTRACT Amid intensified global talent competition and domestic demographic pressures, China, Japan and South Korea (hereafter, ‘Korea’) have expanded their international student policies beyond attraction and recruitment to include stronger measures for post‐study employment and retention, repositioning international students as strategic populations for the broader state agenda. Drawing on an interpretive comparative analysis of official policy documents, this study examines how the shared policy turn is articulated in China, Japan and Korea through agenda framing, goal setting and policy instrument mix. The findings show that this shared turn has not followed a common model, but rather distinct policy logics: selective channelling in China, where international graduates are incorporated selectively through talent‐oriented and eligibility‐based channels linked to national development priorities; coordinated labour‐market incorporation in Japan, where policy emphasises facilitated transition into domestic employment; and region‐linked settlement in Korea, where employment and retention are tied more explicitly to regional revitalisation and settlement. title: The Taboo of Power Dynamics in Doctoral Supervision: Cross‐Cultural Insights From Australia, South Africa and the South Pacific Region
text_snippet: The Taboo of Power Dynamics in Doctoral Supervision: Cross‐Cultural Insights From Australia, South Africa and the South Pacific Region ABSTRACT This review article explores the often‐unspoken power dynamics between doctoral supervisors and students, focusing on the taboo surrounding the discussion of these imbalances. Power differentials in supervisory relationships significantly influence the doctoral experience. However, historical, cultural and institutional norms often prevent open discussions about these power structures, allowing them to persist unchallenged. Adopting a cross‐cultural perspective, this article examines supervisory power relations across Australia, South Africa and the South Pacific region connected through a consortium in the Next Generation Research SuperVision Project (RSVP), a Research England funded project. Whilst Australian academic culture is often seen as egalitarian, hidden hierarchies persist. In South Africa, power asymmetries are deeply entangled with social and racial histories, whilst in the South Pacific region, respect for authority can inhibit dissent. Framed through the lens of taboo, this article highlights how silences around power impact doctoral education and calls for culturally attuned strategies to address them.

title: Navigating Supervisory Conversations About Gen AI : Taboo and Supervisory Power Dynamics
text_snippet: Navigating Supervisory Conversations About Gen AI : Taboo and Supervisory Power Dynamics ABSTRACT Generative artificial intelligence (gen AI) technologies have disrupted the longstanding norms and practices of education and research in universities, fueling widespread discussions across the humanities, arts and social sciences (HASS) disciplines including in the community of doctoral education. This qualitative study examines how communication about gen AI use takes place in HASS research supervision meetings, and the ways that doctoral supervisors and international doctoral students navigate these conversations. Thematic analysis of interviews with international doctoral students and doctoral supervisors reveals the use of gen AI by international doctoral students as a delicate and often ‘tabooed’ topic in supervision meetings. We argue that gen AI being a taboo topic in supervisory meetings reflects both the ambiguity surrounding the legitimacy of using gen AI in doctoral research, as well as the influence of intersecting supervisory power dynamics, including structural power , epistemic power and relational power . We recommend supervisory communication strategies to critically facilitate the transition to AI in international doctoral education.

title: Institutionalizing Ethics, Encountering Misconduct: A Case From Kazakhstan
text_snippet: Institutionalizing Ethics, Encountering Misconduct: A Case From Kazakhstan ABSTRACT This study examines the emergence of ethically problematic research practices during the establishment of an Institutional Research Ethics Committee (IREC) at a newly founded, research‐intensive university in Kazakhstan. Drawing on semi‐structured interviews with faculty members, IREC members, and institutional leaders involved in the university's formative years, the study explores how institutional, individual, and contextual factors shaped engagement with research ethics governance. The findings identify practices such as bypassing ethics review, retrospective protocol submissions, limited ethics training among IREC members, and passive participation in review processes. While these practices do not always align with narrow definitions of research misconduct (e.g., fabrication, falsification, plagiarism), they represent significant deviations from core research ethics principles, including accountability, protection of human subjects, professional competence, and adherence to institutional regulations. title: Navigating the Invisible Load: Taboos in the Experiences of Female CALD Doctoral Students Balancing Family and Study in Australia
text_snippet: Navigating the Invisible Load: Taboos in the Experiences of Female CALD Doctoral Students Balancing Family and Study in Australia ABSTRACT This study explores unspoken challenges faced by female doctoral students from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) backgrounds in Australia. Drawing on in‐depth interviews with seven CALD women at two Australian universities and guided by Butler's gender performativity, Crenshaw's intersectionality, and postcolonial feminism, we examine how these women negotiate their multiple roles. The analysis reveals three intersecting taboos that shape their academic journeys: the taboo of vulnerability, which discourages disclosing personal or academic struggles; silencing as a result of cultural and gendered expectations, which compels them to manage conflicting scholarly and parenting roles privately; and the stigma surrounding mental health, which compels emotional restraint. These taboos intensify stress and reinforce existing structural inequalities in doctoral education. The paper underscores the need to acknowledge how gendered and cultural expectations are embedded in academic institutions and advocates for reform to create a more inclusive and equitable academic environment for CALD women scholars.

title: Housing Experiences and Inequalities Among Higher Education Students in Portugal: Study‐Related Housing Adequacy in Lisbon and Porto
text_snippet: Housing Experiences and Inequalities Among Higher Education Students in Portugal: Study‐Related Housing Adequacy in Lisbon and Porto ABSTRACT In Europe, rising rental costs and spatial inequalities in urban areas increasingly shape student housing conditions, with implications for student well‐being and access to higher education. This study examines housing conditions among students in Portugal's two largest urban centres, Lisbon and Porto, cities deeply affected by housing shortages, rising rental costs, and competition from tourism and international rental market investment. The aim was to assess whether housing conditions differ between domestic students living in their home region, domestic students displaced from their region of origin (domestic mobile students), and international students. Data were collected through a cross‐sectional online survey ( N = 2929), targeting undergraduate students enrolled at institutions located in Porto and Lisbon metropolitan areas. Welch ANOVAs tested group differences and a generalised ordered logit model assessed whether differences in study‐related housing adequacy persisted after adjusting for rent. title: ‘Almost but Not Quite’: Professional Services Working in Doctoral Education
text_snippet: ‘Almost but Not Quite’: Professional Services Working in Doctoral Education ABSTRACT Professional Services staff who hold doctoral qualifications and remain research‐active can make important contributions to doctoral supervision and scholarly activity. Yet, despite their expertise, they are often formally excluded from doing so because their employment contracts often categorise them as outside the scope of academic activities. These contractual and structural restrictions form an unspoken but pervasive ‘taboo’ within doctoral education, the assumption that only staff on academic contracts are legitimate participants in supervision and scholarly practice. Drawing on the autoethnographic reflections of two such professionals with distinct disciplinary and career trajectories, this article explores how these constraints generate processes of marginalisation and ‘othering’ for doctoral‐qualified Professional Services staff. The paper argues for a more inclusive model of doctoral education that recognises and utilises the supervisory expertise and research contributions of research‐active Professional Services colleagues.

title: Myth or Merit? A Reassessment of the “Monks From Afar” Effect in Taiwan's Dual‐Track Talent Policy in Higher Education
text_snippet: Myth or Merit? A Reassessment of the “Monks From Afar” Effect in Taiwan's Dual‐Track Talent Policy in Higher Education ABSTRACT In response to global talent competition and the goal of building world‐class universities, Taiwan's government introduced talent policies to enhance research capacity and international visibility. This study employs a mixed‐methods design to analyse the distribution of four main awardee types in alignment with Taiwan's dual talent policies and assess their research productivity, impact, and collaboration using bibliometric methods. Semi‐structured interviews are used to illustrate the challenges of policy implementation. Three key findings are presented as follows. First, Yushan and Young Yushan fellows surpass local awardees in research productivity and international engagement. Second, while Outstanding Research Award awardees maintain strong performance in top‐cited publications and FWCI, Young Yushan awardees exhibit higher levels of international collaboration relative to Outstanding Research awardees. Third, challenges such as difficulties in attracting and retaining international scholars, limited campus internationalisation, and significant compensation disparities between award systems continue to undermine the effectiveness of Taiwan's dual talent policy. title: Bridging the Gap Between SDG Learning and Civic Engagement: A Configurational Perspective in the Context of University Social Responsibility
text_snippet: Bridging the Gap Between SDG Learning and Civic Engagement: A Configurational Perspective in the Context of University Social Responsibility ABSTRACT This study challenges the common assumption that learning about the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is consistently associated with civic engagement in higher education. Adopting a configurational perspective, it examines how different learning patterns are associated with variations in participatory outcomes. Drawing on the knowledge–attitude–skills (KAS) framework, the study analyses survey data from undergraduate students within a higher education system shaped by University Social Responsibility (USR) policy initiatives. The findings show that SDG learning does not demonstrate a uniform association with civic engagement. Instead, the relationship varies according to how learning experiences are configured across knowledge, attitudes, and skills. Three configurations are identified: balanced, misaligned, and low engagement. Building on this insight, the study reinterprets the relationship among SDGs, USR, and Global Citizenship Education (GCED) as a mechanism‐based framework. title: ‘I Don't Want to Kill Any More Mice’: Taboo and Silence in PhD Education
text_snippet: ‘I Don't Want to Kill Any More Mice’: Taboo and Silence in PhD Education ABSTRACT Improving the experience and well‐being of doctoral students requires a deep and nuanced understanding of their challenges. Traditionally, researchers have used reactive methods, such as surveys and interviews, to address these issues. However, some topics may be difficult to capture through these approaches, particularly those that are intentionally avoided or hard to discuss openly—what we might call ‘taboo’ topics. In this paper, we propose an approach to addressing this challenge by using nonreactive data sources, particularly from social media platforms and other online forums. We operationalise taboo as topics that are raised as explicitly anonymous questions by doctoral students, suggesting their prohibited or restricted nature. Our goal is twofold: first, to understand the whole range of challenges discussed by doctoral students on social platforms, and second, to determine which of these challenges are considered taboo by comparing explicitly anonymous and nonanonymous questions. By relying on large‐scale computational analysis of social media data, our approach offers a comprehensive and unfiltered view of graduate student concerns and experiences. Our results hi

title: State Roles in Higher Education Governance: Latin American Insights for the Global South
text_snippet: State Roles in Higher Education Governance: Latin American Insights for the Global South ABSTRACT Higher education governance in the Global South develops unevenly, yet how states manage diverse market‐driven systems remains poorly understood. This article examines how five Latin American countries—Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Mexico—have redefined the state's roles, based on a comparative analysis of documents and a framework highlighting five key functions: system design, promotion, regulation, evaluation and financing. The research finds that governance pathways are shaped more by how these functions are connected than by their mere presence. The resulting configurations vary significantly, reflecting different government policy‐making abilities and diverse historical paths. These patterns are seen as signs of structural hybridity—where state guidance, market growth and institutional autonomy coexist—a phenomenon that, as public policy literature shows, extends beyond higher education. The study provides a transferable analytical framework for examining state guidance across the Global South.

title: An Integrated Statistical Methodology Approach to Enrollment Management
text_snippet: An Integrated Statistical Methodology Approach to Enrollment Management ABSTRACT This study examines the decision‐making processes of prospective students and parents to establish an evidence‐based framework for higher education enrollment management. Utilizing a survey of 948 students and 990 parents, the research employs conjoint analysis, factor analysis, and cluster segmentation to identify key institutional choice drivers. Findings reveal that while academic reputation is the most influential attribute, decisions are primarily shaped by three latent constructs: Reputation, Recommendation, and Fit. This paper makes a substantive contribution by operationalizing market orientation through advanced analytics, revealing heterogeneous student segments with distinct motivational profiles. These insights provide university administrators with actionable diagnostics for resource allocation and targeted messaging. Ultimately, the study bridges theoretical understanding and practical application, offering a robust, data‐driven model for improving competitive positioning and recruitment outcomes within the increasingly complex higher education landscape.

title: A Pervasive, Yet Rectifiable Taboo: Addressing the Mental Health Challenges of International Doctoral Students in STEM Fields
text_snippet: A Pervasive, Yet Rectifiable Taboo: Addressing the Mental Health Challenges of International Doctoral Students in STEM Fields ABSTRACT Open discussions about international students' mental health challenges remain a taboo in U.S. doctoral education. The taboo nature of mental health is especially powerful in doctoral environments which celebrate “grit,” resilience, and self‐sufficiency while either tacitly or openly discouraging students from seeking help. This qualitative study investigates the taboo of international doctoral students' mental health challenges by drawing upon multiple interviews with eight international doctoral students working in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) fields at a U.S. research university. Data pertaining to mental health challenges point to four themes: (1) cultural isolation and displacement, (2) financial insecurity, (3) advising relationships, and (4) support networks. Analysing data through the lens of Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory, this article then argues that institutions must consider how to address students' challenges on all five levels—micro, meso, exo, macro, and chrono—to destigmatize the taboo of mental health in doctoral education.

title: The Regulation and Performance of Chinese Private Higher Education in the Stock Market: Dynamics, Impacts and Challenges
text_snippet: The Regulation and Performance of Chinese Private Higher Education in the Stock Market: Dynamics, Impacts and Challenges ABSTRACT This study focuses on stock market‐listed private higher education (PHE) institutions in China, exploring how they have leveraged public listings to break free from traditional funding limitations, facilitate resource integration, and drive educational innovation amid an evolving policy landscape. Concurrently, it examines the complexities arising from the integration of market dynamics with educational missions, including risks to quality assurance, financial vulnerabilities, and potential compromises to educational integrity. Drawing on national policy documents and interview transcripts with multiple stakeholders, this paper maps the developmental trajectory of listed PHE institutions in China and identifies patterns and divergences in how regulatory frameworks and market conditions influence the development of these institutions. The findings not only provide empirical evidence for understanding policy adjustments in China's PHE sector but also offer insights into policy choices related to balancing funding diversification and quality assurance in the emerging higher education system in Asia. title: Geography and Gains of Doctoral Mobility: Origin, Training Site and Employment Location Among Recent PhDs From Chinese Universities
text_snippet: Geography and Gains of Doctoral Mobility: Origin, Training Site and Employment Location Among Recent PhDs From Chinese Universities ABSTRACT The mobility of doctoral graduates shapes both early‐career trajectories and the geography of research talent. In China, doctoral training, research resources and high‐value employment opportunities are concentrated in a limited number of cities, so the transition from doctoral education to first employment is closely structured by educational hierarchy and regional inequality. Using a 2025 survey of doctoral graduates matched to city‐level indicators of economic, research and digital capacity, this study examines doctoral mobility through the linked locations of origin, training site and employment. It distinguishes between the likelihood of taking employment outside the PhD city and the gains associated with destination sorting among inter‐city movers. The findings show that graduates' location after doctoral training is central to subsequent mobility outcomes. Among movers, origin‐to‐employment gains are explained primarily by the extent to which the employment city exceeds the PhD city in economic, research and digital capacity. title: Bridging Local and Global Practices: Examining Internationalisation Strategies in Higher Education
text_snippet: Bridging Local and Global Practices: Examining Internationalisation Strategies in Higher Education ABSTRACT Internationalisation of curriculum, research and service remains a fundamental factor in higher education, where best practices are adopted and contextualised across different educational systems to enhance efficiency and productivity. A plethora of studies have examined how internationalisation has built on local, national and regional policies and practices to harness, complement and harmonise local activities in institutions. However, many researchers and educators have advocated for a more holistic picture of how internationalisation has been contextualised into different sectors and dimensions. title: Between Compliance and Agency: A Comparative Study of University Institutional Research ( IR ) Units Under Government Accountability Pressures in Korea and Japan
text_snippet: Between Compliance and Agency: A Comparative Study of University Institutional Research ( IR ) Units Under Government Accountability Pressures in Korea and Japan ABSTRACT This study explores how institutional research (IR) units in South Korea and Japan are shaped by the complex interaction between government accountability pressures and organisational agency. Based on a comparative qualitative study, we propose a framework comprising four types of organisational responses to accountability pressures, differentiated by the degree of compliance and agency: (I) bureaucratic compliance, (II) strategic compliance, (III) symbolic autonomy and (IV) learning autonomy. In the Korean cases, where universities operate under strong government intervention in evaluation and funding, IR units remain largely in bureaucratic compliance but are gradually moving towards strategic compliance through organisational learning. In the Japanese cases, under weaker external pressure, IR units tend to exhibit symbolic autonomy—formal autonomy without integrative governance. These findings challenge the assumed dichotomy between high compliance and low agency, showing that agency, although bounded, can emerge even under strong accountability constraints, whereas low‐compliance environments do not necessarily foster proactive organisational learning. title: AI Use and Research Integrity in Higher Education: Faculty Perspectives on Opportunities, Challenges, Strategies, and Misconduct
text_snippet: AI Use and Research Integrity in Higher Education: Faculty Perspectives on Opportunities, Challenges, Strategies, and Misconduct ABSTRACT Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly being integrated into academia. Although a great deal has been written about research misconduct, much of this work has focused primarily on Western higher education, with little attention given to the use of AI‐enabled tools in research ethics within non‐Western contexts. This study employed a cross‐sectional online survey with both closed‐ and open‐ended questions, an appropriate design for exploring faculty perceptions of a higher education institution in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Data was collected from 22 faculty members across various disciplines. Findings show that faculty adoption of generative AI tools is primarily driven by perceived usefulness and ease of use for tasks such as writing, editing, idea generation, and data analysis. However, key challenges include the risk of cognitive dependency, production of superficial outputs, loss of originality, and the lack of clear institutional guidance. To mitigate these risks, participants emphasised practices such as human validation of AI‐generated content, multi‐source cross‐verification, and transparent disclosure of AI use in academic work. title: A Qualitative Analysis of the Causes and Consequences of Research Misconduct Among Early‐Career Faculty Members: A Large Public University in Iran
text_snippet: A Qualitative Analysis of the Causes and Consequences of Research Misconduct Among Early‐Career Faculty Members: A Large Public University in Iran ABSTRACT A grounded‐theory study reveals how structural pressures and proximate incentives produce research misconduct among early‐career faculty in Iranian universities. Using 54 semi‐structured interviews (36 doctoral candidates, 10 early‐career faculty, 8 senior professors) and coded official news reports, we used open, axial and selective coding to build a processual model. Distal factors—political pressure, underfunding, unequal infrastructure, regional disparities—interact with proximal drivers: publication‐quantity incentives, intense competition, normalized cheating and academic exploitation. Emergent mechanisms (manuscript‐writing markets, unregulated AI) amplify fabrication, plagiarism and honorary authorship. Harms span individual (psychological strain), organizational (credibility loss, entrenched corruption) and national (erosion of R&D capacity) levels. The study extends empirical focus beyond biomedical fields to social, behavioural and engineering disciplines in an LMIC and proposes policy and practical interventions: revise evaluation criteria, strengthen oversight and training and support vulnerable researchers. title: Doctoral Problems and Taboos: Silence, Well‐Being and Academic Persistence in Czech Doctoral Education
text_snippet: Doctoral Problems and Taboos: Silence, Well‐Being and Academic Persistence in Czech Doctoral Education ABSTRACT This paper examines how the taboos and problems perceived by doctoral students are associated with their well‐being and their intentions to persist in or leave academia. We distinguish between doctoral problems—stressors associated with doctoral study—and doctoral taboos, understood as issues that remain difficult to voice in relationships with supervisors or peers because their disclosure may evoke shame or threaten these relationships. Drawing on a mixed‐methods design conducted in the Czech Republic, we first developed core perceived doctoral problems and taboos based on a qualitative analysis of 21 in‐depth interviews. Doctoral problems and taboos were subsequently examined in a national survey of 190 doctoral students using machine learning models. Financial difficulties constituted the most prevalent doctoral problem, reported by roughly 75% of students. Partial dependence analyses indicated that several doctoral taboos (e.g., finances, parenthood, supervisor quality) were among the strongest predictors of burnout, depression, anxiety, stress and intentions to drop out or leave academia.
